edge_cases.scenario: A consumer disputes a collection account through Experian's online portal. The furnisher receives the ACDV, spends two minutes confirming that the name, address, and balance in its own internal computer file match what it reported, marks the account 'verified,' and reports back to the CRA within 20 days. The consumer had attached a canceled check and a paid-in-full letter to the dispute, which the furnisher never looked at.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node encodes only that the furnisher must 'investigate' and 'review all relevant information the CRA provided,' with no reasonableness standard. Applied as encoded, this furnisher appears fully compliant (it investigated, reviewed, and timely reported), when in fact the near-universal basis for §1681s-2(b) liability is that a perfunctory, records-parroting investigation is not a 'reasonable' investigation. This is the single most common FCRA furnisher fact pattern, and the node would tell the consumer she has no claim when she likely has her strongest one.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer mails a detailed written dispute with supporting documents directly to the debt collector that is reporting the account, and never contacts Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion. The collector ignores the letter and continues reporting. The consumer wants to know what her rights are.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node flags the direct-dispute route as 'a separate duty under §1681s-2(a)(8)' but omits the dispositive fact that §1681s-2(a) duties are not privately enforceable (§1681s-2(c)-(d)) and that routing the dispute through a CRA is a practical prerequisite to any consumer FCRA claim against a furnisher. Describing it as a parallel 'separate duty' misleads a very common class of consumers into thinking their direct dispute preserved a remedy, when it did not and the CRA route must be used (and may be time-barred by the time they learn otherwise).

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer disputes a debt-buyer's tradeline through a CRA, asserting not that the balance or payment history is wrong but that the assignment chain is defective so the debt buyer does not legally own the debt and that the debt is beyond the statute of limitations. The furnisher confirms its purchase records and verifies the tradeline.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's rule ('if inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable after reinvestigation: modify, delete, or block') contains no factual-inaccuracy limitation. Many circuits hold that furnishers have no §1681s-2(b) duty to resolve purely legal disputes about validity, ownership, or enforceability (e.g., Chuluunbat/Denan line of cases), so verification is not a violation. Disputes framed as 'I don't owe this / they don't own it' are extremely common against debt buyers, and the node would tell such a consumer the furnisher was required to delete.

'Particular debt' means each individual debt in collection, except that student loan debts serviced under a single account number when obtained by the collector are treated as one debt.

results.derivation_summary: Section 1692e broadly bars a debt collector from using any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt, and then lists sixteen non-exhaustive examples of violations. These include falsely implying government affiliation or endorsement (1, 9, 16); misrepresenting the character, amount, or legal status of a debt or the fees/services involved (2); falsely posing as an attorney (3); threatening arrest, seizure, garnishment, or other action that is unlawful or not actually intended (4, 5); misstating the effect of selling or transferring the debt (6); falsely accusing the consumer of a crime or disgraceful conduct (7); reporting or threatening to report credit information known to be false, including failing to note that a debt is disputed (8); using deception to collect or to obtain consumer information (10); falsely claiming accounts went to innocent purchasers (12); misrepresenting whether documents are legal process or require action (13, 15); using a business name other than the collector's true name (14); and failing to give the 'mini-Miranda' disclosures (11). Under the current Reg F version, 12 C.F.R. § 1006.18(e), the collector must disclose in the initial communication that it is attempting to collect a debt and that information obtained will be used for that purpose (repeating it in the first written communication if the initial one was oral), must state in each later communication that it is from a debt collector, and is excused from these disclosures only in a formal pleading in a legal action. These duties apply only to a 'debt collector' as defined in § 1692a(6) collecting a consumer 'debt' as defined in § 1692a(5).

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner disputes deceptive statements in letters from her mortgage servicer, which acquired servicing rights (and the loan) while she was current and only began collection activity after she later defaulted. She is neither dealing with the original lender nor with a classic third-party collection agency or debt buyer of charged-off paper.
edge_cases.gap_description: The threshold predicate and checklist frame the coverage question as a binary: original creditor collecting in its own name (exempt) vs. third-party collector or debt buyer (covered). Section 1692a(6)(F)(iii) exempts persons collecting a debt that was not in default at the time it was obtained -- the standard servicer/assignee exclusion. A servicer is neither an 'original creditor' nor a 'debt buyer' as encoded, so the rule would sweep it in as covered and tell the consumer she has an FDCPA claim when the entity is likely outside the Act entirely. Mortgage and student-loan servicing complaints are among the most common consumer debt scenarios.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sends dunning letters and then files a state collection suit on a credit-card debt on which the consumer last paid nine years ago, in a state with a four-year limitations period. The letters and complaint contain no overtly false statements about amount, identity, or affiliation, and the collector gave the mini-Miranda.
edge_cases.gap_description: Filing or threatening suit on a time-barred debt (and, in many courts, dunning on it without disclosure) is a core §1692e(2)(A)/(5)/(10) theory, but neither the catalog gloss nor the completeness checklist asks about the age of the debt, the date of last payment, or the applicable limitations period. Working the checklist as written -- exact wording, threats actually intended, mini-Miranda -- yields 'no violation' for one of the most common and strongest real-world §1692e claims. Stale-debt collection is extremely common.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer receives an otherwise accurate collection letter from a third-party agency on a household credit-card debt; the letter states an incorrect date of last payment and says 'interest may continue to accrue,' though the account is static and no interest is being added. The consumer sues on that basis alone.
edge_cases.gap_description: The encoding treats any factual match to a catalog item as an independent violation with no materiality filter and no articulation of the least-sophisticated/unsophisticated-consumer objective standard. Most circuits require the false statement to be material -- capable of influencing the consumer's response to the debt -- and routinely dismiss claims premised on minor, non-influential inaccuracies. As encoded, the rule tells this consumer she has a §1692e(2)(A)/(10) claim when the claim would likely fail, which is the actual pivot in a large share of §1692e litigation.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is sued by a debt buyer in a Texas justice court (small claims) for $6,000 and a default judgment is signed against her; she comes for help 20 days later asking how to reopen it.
edge_cases.gap_description: The encoding hard-codes the TRCP 329b(a) 30-day district/county court deadline. Justice court defaults are governed by TRCP 505.3 (motion to reinstate or motion for new trial due within 14 days of the judgment, with appeal by trial de novo within 21 days). A justice-court defendant told she has 30 days would be told she is timely when her only Rule 505.3 window has already closed, and would miss the de novo appeal route as well. Debt-collection defaults in justice court are among the most common default judgments in Texas, so this is not a corner case.

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant first learns of a default judgment 55 days after it was signed, when his bank account is frozen by a writ of garnishment; the clerk's notice of judgment went to an old address and he never received it.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist treats "more than 30 days since signing" as a dispositive gate that forecloses the path. TRCP 306a(4)-(5) restarts the 30-day period from the date the party acquired actual knowledge or received notice (up to 90 days after signing), on a sworn motion establishing the date of notice. The encoded rule would tell a defendant with a live, timely-if-properly-invoked motion for new trial that his path is foreclosed — an affirmatively wrong answer in the single most common late-discovery scenario (judgment discovered via garnishment, abstract of judgment, or wage withholding).

The node frames the three-factor test as the operative standard and the 30-day gate as absolutely foreclosing, so a never-served defendant would be told both that he must satisfy factors he need not satisfy and that he has no remaining remedy when he in fact has two. Defective/substituted service is the leading cause of Texas default judgments, so this is squarely material.
